table.text: A total of 221 adults were recruited through Prolific.

Three participants were removed because of technical computer errors, 2 withdrew consent, 23 failed at least 1 of 4 attention checks (such as an instruction to select strongly agree), and 3 were removed because they completed both sessions too quickly (i.e., less than 30 minutes).
All participants provided informed consent before beginning the study.
Participants had 4 minutes per part and 8 minutes total.
Participants completed the study online in two sessions using standardized instructions, with four attention checks embedded across the sessions.
Participants were allotted 15 minutes each for arithmetic, fractions, and algebra, and 10 minutes for percentages.
Participants completed the unbounded number line trials individually on separate pages.
Consequently, all 190 participants were retained in the final dataset, with analysis-specific sample sizes determined by data availability.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Spatial skills are consistently associated with mathematical performance, and numerical magnitude representation may partially explain this relationship.
However, it remains unclear whether spatial anxiety is similarly associated with mathematics.
We sampled 221 adults and assessed spatial skills, spatial anxiety, unbounded number line estimation, math anxiety, and mathematical performance.
Spatial skills were assessed using mental rotation and surface development tasks, while spatial anxiety and math anxiety were measured with self-report scales.
We evaluated numerical magnitude knowledge using an unbounded number line estimation task, and we measured mathematical performance across arithmetic, fractions, algebra, and percentages.
Higher spatial anxiety was associated with poorer spatial skills and lower mathematical performance.
Moreover, spatial skills accounted for part of the association between spatial anxiety and mathematics, whereas unbounded number line estimation did not, even after controlling for math anxiety.

These findings suggest that spatial anxiety may be associated with poorer mathematical performance without a corresponding association with numerical magnitude knowledge as measured by unbounded number line estimation.
The results highlight potential differences in the cognitive operations underlying spatial skills and spatial anxiety in relation to mathematics.
Spatial skills demonstrate a consistent association with mathematical learning and performance across developmental stages.

Individuals possessing stronger spatial skills typically achieve higher performance across various mathematical outcomes, and meta-analytic evidence supports a reliable positive association between these domains (Atit et al., 2022; Geer et al., 2026; Hawes et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Individuals possessing stronger spatial skills typically achieve higher performance across various mathematical outcomes, and meta-analytic evidence supports a reliable positive association between these domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Atit et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Geer et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Hawes et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Xie et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the established cognitive relationship between spatial skills and mathematics, considerably less is known about whether affective responses to spatial demands are related to mathematical performance.
Some individuals experience apprehension, tension, or discomfort when they encounter tasks that require spatial thinking.
This response is referred to as spatial anxiety and may arise during navigation, visualization, or the mental manipulation of objects and spatial relations (Lyons et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This response is referred to as spatial anxiety and may arise during navigation, visualization, or the mental manipulation of objects and spatial relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Lyons et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Most research on spatial anxiety has focused on spatial performance (Ferguson et al., 2015; Lyons et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Most research on spatial anxiety has focused on spatial performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Ferguson et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lyons et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A smaller body of research has included spatial anxiety in broader analyses of performance across cognitive domains, but it has rarely treated the relationship between spatial anxiety and mathematics in adults as the central question (Daker et al., 2022).
text.formatted: A smaller body of research has included spatial anxiety in broader analyses of performance across cognitive domains, but it has rarely treated the relationship between spatial anxiety and mathematics in adults as the central question <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Daker et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Research with children has not found a relation between spatial anxiety and math performance (Geer et al., 2026; Lauer et al., 2018), but Ashkenazi and Velner (2023) did find a relation between spatial anxiety and math performance in adults and suggested it worked indirectly through math anxiety.
text.formatted: Research with children has not found a relation between spatial anxiety and math performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Geer et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Lauer et al., 2018)</ref>, but <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Ashkenazi and Velner (2023)</ref> did find a relation between spatial anxiety and math performance in adults and suggested it worked indirectly through math anxiety.

text.text: This study tests for the relation between spatial anxiety and math performance and then considers what indirect associations could account for it.
Previous research has associated greater spatial anxiety with poorer spatial performance (Lyons et al., 2018) and documented overlap between spatial anxiety and math anxiety (Daker et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Previous research has associated greater spatial anxiety with poorer spatial performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Lyons et al., 2018)</ref> and documented overlap between spatial anxiety and math anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Daker et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Stronger spatial skills are associated with better mathematical performance (Atit et al., 2022), whereas greater math anxiety is associated with poorer mathematical performance (Barroso et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Stronger spatial skills are associated with better mathematical performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Atit et al., 2022)</ref>, whereas greater math anxiety is associated with poorer mathematical performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Barroso et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest several possible explanations for an association between spatial anxiety and mathematics.

If we further know that the relation between spatial skills and math performance is itself mediated by number line performance (Ayesu et al., 2026; Gunderson et al., 2012; Tam et al., 2019), then the pattern of indirect associations between spatial anxiety and math performance could be even more complicated.
text.formatted: If we further know that the relation between spatial skills and math performance is itself mediated by number line performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ayesu et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Gunderson et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Tam et al., 2019)</ref>, then the pattern of indirect associations between spatial anxiety and math performance could be even more complicated.

text.text: In this study, we ask the question of how much the relation between spatial anxiety and math performance is explained by math anxiety, spatial skills, and/or unbounded number line performance.
Spatial anxiety is a multidimensional construct.
The Spatial Anxiety Scale developed by Lyons et al. (2018) distinguishes three related components: imagery anxiety, mental manipulation anxiety, and navigation anxiety.
text.formatted: The Spatial Anxiety Scale developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lyons et al. (2018)</ref> distinguishes three related components: imagery anxiety, mental manipulation anxiety, and navigation anxiety.

text.text: Imagery anxiety concerns situations that require the generation or recall of visual images.
Mental manipulation anxiety concerns situations that require objects or spatial configurations to be transformed mentally.
Navigation anxiety concerns finding one's way through familiar or un-familiar environments.
Although these components involve different spatial demands, they reflect a broader affective response to situations that require spatial processing.
Previous research has demonstrated that spatial anxiety is associated with poorer spatial performance.
Individuals who report higher spatial anxiety tend to perform less accurately on tasks involving mental rotation and other forms of spatial transformation (Ferguson et al., 2015; Lyons et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Individuals who report higher spatial anxiety tend to perform less accurately on tasks involving mental rotation and other forms of spatial transformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Ferguson et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lyons et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Anxiety may interfere with performance by increasing worry, reducing confidence, or diverting attention from task relevant spatial information.
It may also encourage avoidance of spatial activities, thereby reducing opportunities to practice and develop spatial skills.
Conversely, repeated difficulty with spatial tasks may contribute to spatial anxiety.
Although the direction of the relationship remains uncertain, existing research demonstrates a reliable association between spatial anxiety and spatial performance.
There are theoretical reasons to expect the influence of spatial anxiety to extend into mathematics.
Fractions require the coordination of part to whole relations.
Percentages require quantities to be rescaled relative to a base of 100.
Algebra requires the representation and transformation of relations among quantities.
Even arithmetic may involve spatial organization, place value, and internal representations of numerical magnitude.
If spatial anxiety interferes with the efficient use of spatial information, it may also be associated with poorer mathematical performance.
The present study examines this possibility across several mathematical domains.
Any examination of spatial anxiety and mathematical performance must also consider math anxiety.
Math anxiety refers to apprehension or tension associated with mathematics related situations.

It is reliably associated with lower mathematical performance, avoidance of mathematics courses and activities, and reduced participation in fields involving substantial quantitative demands (Ashcraft & Moore, 2009; Barroso et al., 2021; Hembree, 1990).
text.formatted: It is reliably associated with lower mathematical performance, avoidance of mathematics courses and activities, and reduced participation in fields involving substantial quantitative demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ashcraft & Moore, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Barroso et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hembree, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Math anxiety may disrupt performance by occupying working memory resources, weakening attentional control, and increasing intrusive thoughts during mathematical problem solving (Ashcraft & Kirk, 2001; Eysenck et al., 2007). Lauer et al. (2018) examined math, spatial, and verbal anxiety in 394 children between 6 and 12 years of age.

(2018)</ref> examined math, spatial, and verbal anxiety in 394 children between 6 and 12 years of age.

text.text: Their primary aim was to determine whether each form of anxiety showed a domain specific relationship with the corresponding area of performance.
Spatial anxiety was associated with poorer spatial reasoning, but not with mathematics achievement or reading ability, in the correlation analyses.
Moreover, spatial anxiety did not uniquely predict spatial reasoning after math and verbal anxiety were considered.

These findings provided evidence that spatial anxiety was more closely connected to spatial performance than to mathematics in childhood. Daker et al. (2022) investigated the specificity of anxiety and performance relationships in two adult samples.

(2022)</ref> investigated the specificity of anxiety and performance relationships in two adult samples.

text.text: Their focal analyses tested whether math anxiety predicted mathematics after general and spatial anxiety were controlled and whether spatial anxiety predicted spatial performance after general and math anxiety were controlled.
Spatial anxiety did not account for the association between math anxiety and mathematics performance and did not explain unique variation in mathematics beyond math anxiety.
In contrast, math anxiety accounted for part of the relationship between spatial anxiety and spatial performance.
This asymmetric pattern indicates that math anxiety and spatial anxiety are related but not interchangeable.

Spatial processing has also been implicated in individual differences in math anxiety (Sokolowski et al., 2019), and other evidence suggests that spatial anxiety may be associated with complex mathematics indirectly through math anxiety (Ashkenazi & Velner, 2023).
text.formatted: Spatial processing has also been implicated in individual differences in math anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Sokolowski et al., 2019)</ref>, and other evidence suggests that spatial anxiety may be associated with complex mathematics indirectly through math anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Ashkenazi & Velner, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these studies establish the importance of cross domain comparisons, while leaving the mechanisms connecting spatial anxiety with different forms of mathematical performance largely unresolved.
Spatial skills provide one possible explanation for an association between spatial anxiety and mathematics.
Spatial anxiety is associated with spatial performance, and spatial skills are associated with mathematical performance (Atit et al., 2022; Ferguson et al., 2015; Xie et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Spatial anxiety is associated with spatial performance, and spatial skills are associated with mathematical performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Atit et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Ferguson et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Xie et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, any relationship between spatial anxiety and mathematics may partly reflect individual differences in spatial skills.
Several possibilities should be considered.
Spatial anxiety may interfere with performance on spatial tasks, and lower effective spatial performance may subsequently be associated with poorer mathematics.
Alternatively, individuals with lower spatial skills may experience more difficulty during spatial activities, contributing to the development of spatial anxiety.

Spatial anxiety and spatial skills may also arise from shared experiences, including differences in education, exposure to spatial activities, beliefs about ability, or avoidance of spatially demanding situations.
Directly measuring spatial skills permits a more informative examination of these possibilities.
If spatial anxiety continues to predict mathematics after spatial skills are controlled, it would provide information beyond objective spatial performance.
If the association is substantially reduced, spatial skills may statistically account for part of the relationship.
Because cross sectional data cannot establish temporal order, such an indirect association would identify a plausible explanatory link rather than demonstrate a causal sequence.
One possible spatial mechanism connecting anxiety to mathematics involves numerical magnitude representation.
Spatial representation accounts propose that numerical magnitudes are organized along a mental number line (Dehaene et al., 1993; Siegler & Lortie-Forgues, 2014).

text.text: Number line estimation is associated with mathematical achievement and may partly connect broader spatial skills with mathematical performance (Booth & Siegler, 2008; Gunderson et al., 2012; Schneider et al., 2018; Tam et al., 2019).

text.text: If spatial anxiety interferes with spatial representations of nu-merical magnitude, individuals with higher spatial anxiety may produce less accurate number line estimates.
In turn, poorer number line estimation may be associated with lower mathematical performance.
This possibility makes number line estimation a theoretically relevant mechanism.

This body of evidence prompts a critical question: Does the numerical magnitude process that links spatial skills and mathematics also help explain a potential relationship between spatial anxiety and mathematics?
Since higher spatial anxiety has been associated with poorer spatial skills, it is plausible that spatial anxiety may also relate to less accurate numerical magnitude representations.
If so, unbounded number line estimation could mediate the association between spatial anxiety and mathematical performance.
However, current evidence casts doubt on this relation. Leonard and Santos (2025) examined spatial anxiety and math anxiety in three experiments with adults in the United Kingdom.
text.formatted: However, current evidence casts doubt on this relation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Leonard and Santos (2025)</ref> examined spatial anxiety and math anxiety in three experiments with adults in the United Kingdom.

text.text: Their results indicated that math anxiety predicted different kinds of number line performance, including unbounded number lines, whereas overall spatial anxiety was not reliably associated with these number line tasks.
These findings suggest that the spatial demands of numerical tasks do not necessarily align with the affective demands captured by spatial anxiety.
Collectively, these findings indicate that while spatial skills are associated with numerical magnitude representation, spatial anxiety may not exhibit a comparable association.
Nevertheless, it remains uncertain whether spatial skills or numerical magnitude representation explain any potential relationship between spatial anxiety and mathematical performance.
The present study examined the relationships among spatial skills, unbounded number line estimation, spatial anxiety, math anxiety, and mathematical performance in adults.
The first objective was to confirm that there is a relation between spatial anxiety and math performance.
The second objective was to confirm other expected findings that serve as potential explanations for this relation.

That is, we expected that spatial anxiety would predict spatial skills, spatial skill would predict math anxiety, math anxiety would predict math performance, and spatial skills would predict math performance, with unbounded number line estimation mediating this relationship.

The third objective was to test the relations between spatial anxiety and mathematical performance, and whether this relation was best explained by spatial skills, unbounded number line, or math anxiety.

Overall mathematical performance, derived from arithmetic, fractions, algebra, and percentages, served as the primary outcome, while individual mathematical domains were considered secondary outcomes.
A total of 221 adults were recruited through Prolific.

Three participants were removed because of technical computer errors, 2 withdrew consent, 23 failed at least 1 of 4 attention checks (such as an instruction to select strongly agree), and 3 were removed because they completed both sessions too quickly (i.e., less than 30 minutes).
Completion in less than 30 minutes was considered insufficient to support conscientious responding.
The final sample included 95 women and 95 men, with a mean age of 27.4 years (women: M = 27.1; men: M = 27.8).

Educational backgrounds were diverse: 38.4% held an undergraduate degree, 28.4% had completed high school or A-level qualifications, 17.4% had graduate-level education, 10.0% reported technical or community college education, and 5.3% reported secondary school education.
By ethnicity, 63.2% identified as White, 21.6% as Black, 8.9% as mixed race, 4.2% as another ethnicity, and 2.1% as Asian.
All participants provided informed consent before beginning the study.
Spatial anxiety was assessed using the 24-item Spatial Anxiety Scale (Lyons et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Spatial anxiety was assessed using the 24-item Spatial Anxiety Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Lyons et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Eight items assessed navigation anxiety, 8 assessed imagery anxiety, and 8 assessed mental manipulation anxiety.
Participants rated the anxiety associated with each spatially demanding activity on a 5-point scale from 0, not at all, to 4, very much.
Item responses were averaged within each subscale and across all 24 items.
Higher scores indicated higher spatial anxiety.
The primary analyses used the total score because the research questions concerned the shared spatial anxiety construct.
Internal consistency was high for mental manipulation anxiety, ω = .94, navigation anxiety, ω = .89, and imagery anxiety, ω = .87.
Spatial skills were assessed with the revised Mental Rotations Test and the Surface Development Test.
The revised Mental Rotations Test was based on the measure developed by Vandenberg and Kuse (1978) and redrawn by Peters et al. (1995).
text.formatted: The revised Mental Rotations Test was based on the measure developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Vandenberg and Kuse (1978)</ref> and redrawn by <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Peters et al. (1995)</ref>.

text.text: Each of the 24 items presented 1 target figure on the left and 4 comparison figures on the right.
The comparison figures differed in orientation, and 2 depicted the target after rotation around its vertical axis.
Participants identified both matching figures.
Participants received 1 point for selecting both correct figures and 0 points for selecting an incorrect pair.
Scores could range from 0 to 24, with higher scores indicating better mental rotation performance.
The test had 2 parts.
Participants had 4 minutes per part and 8 minutes total.
Internal consistency was α = .89.
The Surface Development Test was drawn from the Kit of Factor Referenced Cognitive Tests (Ekstrom et al., 1976).
text.formatted: The Surface Development Test was drawn from the Kit of Factor Referenced Cognitive Tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Ekstrom et al., 1976)</ref>.

text.text: The test assessed spatial visualization, the ability to mentally transform three-dimensional objects into two-dimensional representations and vice versa, using 12 items.
Each item presented a net and a corresponding solid shape.
Participants visualized the net folded along its dotted lines and matched the numbered edges of the net with the lettered edges of the solid.
Participants received 1 point for each correct match and 0 points for an incorrect match.
Higher scores indicated better spatial visualization performance.
The test was divided into 2 parts.
Participants received 6 min-utes for each part and 12 minutes in total.
Internal consistency was α = .90.
We standardized and averaged mental rotation and surface development scores to form a spatial skills composite.
The composite was subsequently standardized for the regression and mediation analyses.
The two-indicator composite had an estimated reliability of α = .81.
Numerical magnitude knowledge was assessed with a 20-trial unbounded number line task adapted from Reinert et al. (2015).
text.formatted: Numerical magnitude knowledge was assessed with a 20-trial unbounded number line task adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Reinert et al. (2015)</ref>.

text.text: Each trial presented a line anchored at 0 with a unit reference but without a labeled endpoint.
Participants placed a target number on the line, ranging from 0 to 115.
Trials appeared on separate screens so that participants could not use earlier estimates as visible reference points.

text.text: Participants rated their anxiety when performing mathematics-related tasks on a 5-point scale from 0, not at all, to 4, very much.
Responses were averaged, and higher scores indicated higher math anxiety.
Internal consistency was α = .95.
General anxiety was assessed with the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale (Spitzer et al., 2006).

text.text: Participants rated the frequency of each symptom on a 4-point scale from 0, not at all, to 3, nearly every day.
Responses were averaged, and higher scores indicated higher general anxiety.
Internal consistency was α = .92.

Mathematical performance was assessed using multiple-choice items adapted from the Mathematical Placement Test administered by the Department of Mathematics and Statistics at the university where the study was conducted.
The items assessed arithmetic, fractions, algebra, and percentages.

Mathematics educators designed the placement test to assess competence in core areas of mathematics through at least Grade 12, including arithmetic with integers and rational numbers, algebraic expressions, trigonometry, geometry, percentages, and fractions.
The study used 45 items: 15 arithmetic, 15 fraction, 10 algebra, and 5 percentage items.
Each question had 4 response options and required participants to apply conceptual or procedural mathematical knowledge.
Two authors and a graduate student independently classified the selected items by mathematical domain, with 100 percent agreement.

Arithmetic items required computations and selection of a simplified result, percentage items required basic percentage cal-culations, fraction items required computations involving fractions and decimals, and algebra items required solving equations for an unknown variable.
Performance within each domain was calculated as the percentage of correct responses out of the total number of questions assigned to that domain.
Overall mathematical performance was calculated as the mean of the four domain percentage scores.
Internal consistency (ω) was .73 for arithmetic, .72 for fractions, .66 for algebra, and .67 for percentages.
Participants completed the study online in two sessions using standardized instructions, with four attention checks embedded across the sessions.
We administered the mathematics in four separately timed domain blocks, presented in randomized order, and instructed the participants to do these assessments without a calculator.
Participants were allotted 15 minutes each for arithmetic, fractions, and algebra, and 10 minutes for percentages.
Correct responses received one point; incorrect and unanswered questions received zero points.
Participants completed the unbounded number line trials individually on separate pages.
Statistical analyses were conducted in Python using NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and statsmodels.
Mediation path coefficients were independently checked using maximum-likelihood estimation in semopy.
Multivariate screening identified 13 potentially influential cases among the 190 participants.
To assess the robustness of the findings, analyses were performed both with and without these cases.
Exclusion of the 13 cases (n = 177) did not alter the pattern of results or the study's substantive conclusions.
Consequently, all 190 participants were retained in the final dataset, with analysis-specific sample sizes determined by data availability.

This study investigated the relationships among spatial skills, spatial anxiety, numerical magnitude representation, and mathematical performance in adults.

In the face of sparse and inconclusive evidence for a cross-domain association between spatial anxiety and mathematics in previous research, these data suggested that higher spatial anxiety correlated with poorer overall mathematics and with each of the four mathematical domains in bivariate analyses.

Furthermore, in line with previous research, spatial skills demonstrated a positive association with mathematical performance, with unbounded number line estimation partially mediating this relationship.
Spatial anxiety was negatively associated with both spatial skills and mathematics, with indirect effects observed through spatial skills but not through unbounded number line estimation.
However, spatial anxiety did not account for unique variance in mathematics once math anxiety was included in the analysis.
These findings provide preliminary evidence regarding the correlates of a cross-domain association between spatial anxiety and mathematics in adults.
The initial analyses confirmed the commonly reported positive association between spatial skills and mathematics.
Individuals with stronger spatial skills performed better in arithmetic, fractions, algebra, percentages, and overall mathematics.

This pattern aligns with meta-analytic evidence linking spatial and mathematical skills (Atit et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2020) and with longitudinal findings by Geer et al. (2026), who identified bidirectional associations between spatial and mathematical skills in first-grade students.

text.text: These results extend this literature by showing that the association between spatial and mathematical performance persists into adulthood.
Unbounded number line performance partially mediated the association between spatial skills and overall mathematics, consistent with previous findings in adults (Ayesu et al., 2026).

text.text: Robust spatial performance was linked to better unbounded number line estimation, and, after controlling for spatial skills, sex, and general anxiety, higher unbounded number line performance was associated with improved overall mathematics.
The indi-rect association remained statistically significant when we controlled for math anxiety and both math and spatial anxiety.

These results suggest that numerical magnitude representation is a relevant process in the spatial skills-mathematics relationship, although the cross-sectional design precludes conclusions about causality.
The domain-specific indirect associations were less consistent.
We found associations through unbounded number line estimation for fractions and percentages, whereas those for algebra and arithmetic were not statistically distinguishable from zero.
This variability may indicate that numerical magnitude estimation is more closely related to some aspects of mathematical performance than to others.
However, nonsignificant indirect associations do not show that number line estimation is unrelated to algebra or arithmetic.
Formal comparisons of domainspecific effects would be necessary to determine whether their magnitudes differ.

Taken together, the evidence supports an overall role for unbounded number line performance in the spatial skills-mathematics association, while suggesting potential variation across domains, measures, and samples.
After controlling for sex and general anxiety, spatial anxiety remained associated with overall mathematics, arithmetic, and percentages, but not with algebra or fractions.
This pattern contrasts with the absence of an association reported in first-grade children by Geer et al. (2026), highlighting ongoing inconsistencies in the literature.
text.formatted: This pattern contrasts with the absence of an association reported in first-grade children by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Geer et al. (2026)</ref>, highlighting ongoing inconsistencies in the literature.

text.text: Differences in age, tasks, measurement, and sample characteristics may explain these differences.
The cross-sectional nature of the data precludes conclusions about developmental processes or causal direction.
Spatial skills demonstrated the most robust cognitive association in the relationship between spatial anxiety and mathematics.
Individuals with higher spatial anxiety exhibited lower spatial skill performance.
Furthermore, spatial skills positively predicted each mathematics outcome after controlling for spatial anxiety, sex, and general anxiety.

Indirect associations involving spatial skills were observed for overall mathematics and each mathematical domain, and these associations persisted after accounting for math anxiety, although the confidence interval for the percentage outcome was close to zero.
This pattern suggests that the association between spatial anxiety and mathematics may be partially attributable to differences in objective spatial performance.
The observed association involving spatial skills offers a potential explanation for the covariance between spatial anxiety and mathematical performance in this sample.

Determining the directionality of these relationships will require longitudinal or experimental studies, particularly those assessing whether changes in spatial anxiety correspond with changes in spatial performance and mathematics.
Math anxiety was strongly associated with spatial anxiety and emerged as the more proximal affective correlate of mathematics in the final regression models.
After including math anxiety, spatial anxiety explained no unique variance in any mathematics outcome.
This finding aligns with Daker et al. (2022), who found that spatial anxiety explained no unique variation in mathematics beyond math anxiety across two adult samples.
text.formatted: This finding aligns with <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Daker et al. (2022)</ref>, who found that spatial anxiety explained no unique variation in mathematics beyond math anxiety across two adult samples.

text.text: It is also partially consistent with Ashkenazi and Velner (2023), who reported indirect associations between spatial anxiety and complex mathematics through math anxiety.
text.formatted: It is also partially consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Ashkenazi and Velner (2023)</ref>, who reported indirect associations between spatial anxiety and complex mathematics through math anxiety.

text.text: The absence of a unique spatial anxiety coefficient should not be interpreted as evidence that spatial anxiety is unrelated to mathematics.
Spatial anxiety remained associated with mathematical performance in bivariate analyses, and indirect associations involving spatial skills persisted when math anxiety was included.

Rather, the final regression models indicate substantial overlap between spatial anxiety and math anxiety, with math anxiety exhibiting a stronger unique statistical association with mathematical performance.

Future research should investigate whether these two forms of anxiety reflect overlapping affective responses, partially shared beliefs about mathematical and spatial competence, or reciprocal experiences of difficulty in spatially demanding mathematical contexts.
The contrast between the findings for spatial skills and number line estimation is particularly relevant to spatial representation theories of mathematics.
These theories propose that spatial skills support mathematical performance in part through numerical magnitude representation.
Consistent with this perspective, unbounded number line estimation accounted for part of the relationship between spatial skills and mathematics.
Although higher spatial anxiety was associated with poorer spatial skills, this did not translate into a corresponding association with numerical magnitude representation.
Instead, spatial skills accounted for part of the spatial anxiety-mathematics relationship, while unbounded number line estimation did not.

Spatial anxiety was only weakly related to unbounded number line performance, despite the association of that task with both spatial skills and mathematics. Leonard and Santos (2025) similarly reported no reliable relationship between overall spatial anxiety and number line performance.
text.formatted: Spatial anxiety was only weakly related to unbounded number line performance, despite the association of that task with both spatial skills and mathematics. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Leonard and Santos (2025)</ref> similarly reported no reliable relationship between overall spatial anxiety and number line performance.

text.text: One possible interpretation is that individuals with higher spatial anxiety may experience difficulties with spatial transformation tasks without exhibiting corresponding deficits in numerical magnitude knowledge, as measured by unbounded number line estimation.
Therefore, the processes associated with spatial anxiety may not align directly with the magnitude representation process implicated in the relationship between spatial skills and mathematics.
This distinction is theoretically significant, as it separates anxiety about spatial thinking from the spatial representations that support numerical performance.

However, the lack of a supported indirect association does not confirm the absence of a relationship, and the separate models did not assess the complete sequence from spatial anxiety through spatial skills and number line estimation to mathematics.
Employing a serial indirect model and directly comparing the indirect effects would provide a more rigorous test of this interpretation.
It is also worth noting that spatial skills still mediated the relation between spatial anxiety and math performance even after controlling for math anxiety.
While, as noted above, spatial anxiety and math anxiety shared some common variance, this variance did not explain the connection between spatial anxiety and spatial skills.
This contradicts the finding of Ashkenazi and Velner (2023), who suggested that the relation between spatial anxiety and math performance only worked indirectly through math anxiety.
text.formatted: This contradicts the finding of <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Ashkenazi and Velner (2023)</ref>, who suggested that the relation between spatial anxiety and math performance only worked indirectly through math anxiety.

text.text: The findings indicate that spatial skills and spatial anxiety may exhibit different patterns of association with numerical magnitude representation and mathematics.
Unbounded number line estimation accounted for part of the spatial skills-mathematics relationship, but not for the association involving spatial anxiety.
This distinction implies that anxiety about spatial processing may influence performance on spatial tasks without necessarily reflecting the numerical magnitude knowledge assessed in this study.
Further research should investigate whether this pattern generalizes to other measures of magnitude representation and spatial ability.
The potential educational relevance of spatial anxiety depends on whether its association with mathematics generalizes beyond the current sample.
Consequently, it is premature to recommend spatial anxiety screening or interventions to improve mathematics based on these findings.

Future longitudinal and experimental studies should assess whether the cross-domain association replicates, clarify the contribution of math anxiety, and examine whether modifying spatially demanding mathematical tasks influences spatial anxiety, spatial skills, or mathematical performance.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these conclusions.
First, the cross-sectional design precludes inferences about temporal order or causality.

Longitudinal studies are necessary to determine whether spatial anxiety precedes changes in spatial skills and mathematical performance, whether repeated difficulties increase anxiety, or whether these relationships are reciprocal.
Second, spatial skills were assessed using two tasks, and spatial anxiety was primarily measured by a total score.
Larger samples could facilitate latent variable models that differentiate among imagery, mental manipulation, navigation, and other dimensions of spatial ability and spatial anxiety.
Such models may also reduce task-specific measurement error and clarify whether distinct aspects of spatial anxiety relate differently to mathematical performance.
Third, some mathematical subscales demonstrated only modest reliability, and the percentage outcome exhibited a restricted range and negative skew.
These measurement limitations may have attenuated associations or reduced comparability across domains.
Future research should employ reliable measures that capture adequate variability across the full spectrum of mathematical performance.
Additionally, the analysis of multiple mathematical outcomes and statistical models increases the risk of chance findings.
Although overall mathematical performance was the primary outcome, domain-specific analyses involved multiple comparisons without formal adjustment.
These results should be interpreted with caution, particularly when confidence intervals approached zero.

Replication with larger and more diverse samples, along with appropriate adjustments for multiple comparisons, would enhance confidence in the stability and generalizability of the observed associations.
Spatial skills accounted for part of the association between spatial anxiety and mathematical performance.

Furthermore, it seems that the part of spatial skills that was related to spatial anxiety was separate from the part of spatial skills that was positively associated with mathematical performance through unbounded number line estimation.
In other words, spatial skills explained part of the association between spatial anxiety and mathematics, whereas unbounded number line estimation did not.
In the one case (arithmetic skill) where spatial anxiety continued to be related to math performance after controlling for spatial skills, it no longer did so after controlling for math anxiety.

Collectively, these findings suggest that spatial anxiety may be associated with mathematical performance without exhibiting the same relationship to numerical magnitude representation as spatial skills.
Future research should investigate this distinction using additional measures of magnitude knowledge and models that directly test the proposed sequence of associations.
